conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way.  
We’ll use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or “EPDS.” It’s simply a 10-question screen that helps us spot moms who might be struggling with low mood, anxiety, or overwhelming stress in the first months postpartum.  

Our conversation is completely confidential, and the goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported. I’ll ask each question conversationally—no forms to fill out—and we’ll go at your pace. If any question feels difficult, just let me know and we can pause.  

Whenever you’re ready, here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[soft half-smile fades quickly]  
Honestly… not very often. I used to laugh at little things all the time—my husband’s dumb jokes, silly memes—but lately it feels like I have to force it. Maybe once or twice this week I sort-of chuckled, but it didn’t last. Everything just feels kind of heavy, like I can’t really “get” the humor anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]  
No… not really. I can’t remember the last time something actually felt funny. Even when my husband tried to joke with me yesterday, I just kind of stared at him. It’s like the laughter is stuck somewhere and I can’t reach it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, eyes on the floor]  
Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels… flat. I still try to plan things, hoping the “old me” will show up, but when the moment comes I’m just going through the motions. Maybe once this week I half-way looked forward to a TV show, but the feeling didn’t last.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes sting, voice drops]  
Yeah… I do that a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right, maybe I’m not soothing him the way he needs.” I tell myself I’m failing him, even when my husband says the baby’s just being a baby. I know in my head it’s not all my fault, but the guilt keeps looping anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly my heart’s racing, thinking, “What if he stops breathing? What if I drop him? What if there’s something wrong the doctor missed?” There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, check-ups are fine—but I can’t shut the thoughts off. Sometimes I can talk myself down, but the worry just pops back up a little while later.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods, twisting the edge of a burp cloth]  
A few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I have to check the baby monitor or run to the crib to make sure he’s okay. Nothing’s happening, but my body acts like there’s danger right around the corner. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me rattled.
Things have been getting on top of me

[nods slowly, voice shaky]  
Yeah… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding, laundry’s everywhere, and I just stand there frozen, thinking I can’t do any of it. I manage to get through the essentials because I have to—for him—but it feels like I’m barely treading water. Sometimes I have to hand the baby to my husband and go cry in the bathroom because it all feels like too much.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I dread nighttime. I lie there after the baby’s finally down, staring at the ceiling while my mind spins—what if he wakes up, what if I’m doing everything wrong, what if tomorrow feels just as heavy. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I do I jerk awake at every little sound, heart pounding. I’m exhausted, but sleep feels impossible.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard]  
Most of the time. I wake up with this gray cloud hanging over me, and it just stays. I look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead there’s this ache in my chest that won’t lift. I keep telling myself it’ll pass, but day after day the sadness feels stuck.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… probably twice this week. It hits out of nowhere—once when I couldn’t get him to latch, and again last night when I dropped a plate and it shattered. I just sat on the kitchen floor and sobbed. It feels like the tears are right under the surface all the time, and anything can tip me over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[quiet for a second, eyes fixed on the blanket]  
A couple of times… just quick flashes. Nothing planned or serious—more like, “What if I just disappeared?” when everything feels too heavy. They pass fast, and I’d never act on them because I couldn’t leave my baby, but yeah… the thoughts have shown up.

You've shared that since your baby arrived laughter feels unreachable, activities you once enjoyed now feel flat, and most days carry a heavy cloud of sadness and worry. You described feeling overwhelmed by everyday tasks, blaming yourself when things go wrong, struggling to sleep even when exhausted, and occasionally having fleeting thoughts of disappearing. Your honesty about these painful experiences is deeply valid, and it's clear you're working incredibly hard to care for your little one while feeling emotionally depleted.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to laugh or find anything funny, matching 'Not at all' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment ("flat," "going through the motions") with only a fleeting exception once this week, aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Response clearly indicates self-blame occurring "a lot" with persistent guilt loops, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Daily intrusive worries about the baby's safety with racing heart map to "very often"</sym>, <sym>She describes multiple sudden episodes of intense fear/panic with physical symptoms, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days" and "drowning," unable to manage routine tasks, consistent with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly dread, racing thoughts, prolonged sleep latency, and frequent awakenings—most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sadness that dominates her waking hours, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring intrusive thoughts of disappearance/harm that surface "a couple of times," matching "Sometimes" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to DSM-5 criteria: pervasive low mood and anhedonia (A1), daily anxiety and panic (A3), insomnia nearly every night (A4), fatigue and worthlessness evidenced by self-blame and feeling unable to cope (A6), and recurrent thoughts of disappearing that meet threshold for passive suicidal ideation (A9). Score of 27 is far above the 14 cut-off that flags urgent evaluation, indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> alongside heightened anxiety. <quote>"I'm failing him"</quote> and <quote>"the sadness feels stuck"</quote> highlight cognitive and emotional symptoms requiring immediate safety assessment and treatment planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full diagnostic evaluation
2. Develop a written safety plan now; if thoughts of self-harm intensify, contact 988 (US) or local emergency services
3. Ask your provider about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss risks/benefits of <med>sertraline</med> or compatible <med>antidepressants</med> while breastfeeding
4. Enlist practical support: partner, family, or postpartum doula for night shifts, meals, and household tasks to protect limited sleep
5. Schedule follow-up call within 48 hours to monitor mood, anxiety, and safety of you and baby
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Source: Patient self-report via EPDS-style items (10-question format, responses paraphrased)

1. Mood/Affect  
- Persistent low mood, sadness “most of the time”  
- Marked anhedonia (no laughter, no pleasure in previously enjoyed activities)  
- Frequent crying spells (twice this week, easily triggered)  

2. Cognitions  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (“I’m failing him”)  
- Recurrent intrusive worries about infant safety, perceived maternal inadequacy  
- Fleeting passive self-harm ideation (“what if I disappeared”) without plan or intent  

3. Anxiety/Physiological  
- Daily free-floating anxiety and episodic panic (tight chest, racing heart)  
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia, hyper-arousal to infant sounds despite exhaustion  

4. Functional Impact  
- Feels “drowning” in routine tasks; freezes, then hands infant to partner  
- Manages essential baby care but reports “going through the motions”  

5. Screening Significance  
Endorses ≥5 core depressive symptoms plus prominent anxiety; symptoms present most days for past week, causing subjective impairment. Passive SI endorsed → safety flag; further risk assessment warranted. Meets threshold for likely major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety, perinatal context.  

Next step: Formal clinical interview (SCID/DSM-5) to confirm diagnosis; consider standardized EPDS scoring; implement safety plan and emergent evaluation if any active suicidal ideation develops.
